planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed onto the soil surface in fall for natural cold-moist stratification over winter; seedlings emerge the following spring but the plant typically does not flower until its second or third year, so patience is required while the large basal rosette develops.

directions: Plant in moist, rich, humus-laden soil in partial shade, mimicking the bottomland woodlands, wooded stream terraces, and lower slopes of wooded bluffs across the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys and the Appalachians where this striking native grows wild. This species is grown chiefly for its bold, kidney-shaped basal leaves on long petioles, which can reach nearly two feet across and give the plant a tropical, architectural presence at the back of a shaded border — distinct from the more common Arnoglossum atriplicifolium, which shares the same vernacular name but has triangular rather than kidney-shaped leaves. In summer, flat-topped clusters of small, dull white to greenish disk flowers rise on tall stalks above the foliage, drawing a notably wide range of small carpenter bees, halictid bees, masked bees, sphecid and eumenine wasps, and syrphid flies. Because it is slow to reach flowering size from seed, established divisions from a nursery give the fastest results in a rich, moist, shaded woodland garden.

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall onto a partially shaded woodland bed; a winter of cold, moist stratification is needed to break dormancy, and seedlings establish a basal rosette the first year before flowering the following season.

directions: Plant in dry to moist, humus-rich, often calcareous soil in partial to full shade; this upright woodland perennial, also classified as Nabalus albus, is found naturally across Canada and the northeastern and upper midwestern United States in mixed woods, thickets, jack pine stands, and rocky shores. Loose, nodding clusters of small, drooping, greenish-white to cream flower heads open from late summer into fall on tall, often purple-tinged stems, providing a late nectar source for bees, beetles, and moths at a time when little else blooms in the shade garden. Milky sap exudes from broken stems, a family trait shared with related lettuce-tribe wildflowers. It self-sows modestly once established and pairs well with ferns and native sedges in a naturalistic woodland planting.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into lean, dry, sandy to rocky acidic soil at a woodland edge; germination and establishment are gradual, and the evergreen basal rosette typically needs a full season before sending up its first flowering stalk.

directions: Plant in lean, dry, sandy or rocky, acidic soil in partial shade to light woodland cover; rattlesnake weed is native to the eastern third of North America, where it forms a low, semi-evergreen rosette of leaves attractively netted with purple-red veins in dry open pine and oak woods, barrens, and trailside openings that defeat richer-soil groundcovers. Leafless flowering stalks rise above the foliage from late spring into summer, each topped with small, bright yellow, dandelion-like flower heads that draw a range of small native bees and other pollinators to nutrient-poor sandy ground. It spreads gradually by short rhizomes to form a tidy, low-maintenance mat, making it a genuinely useful native for the driest, most difficult part-shade spots under oaks and pines. It is not related to the invasive Eurasian hawkweeds sometimes confused with it.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
Digital Atlas of the Virginia Flora

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall onto rocky, well-drained soil at a woodland edge for natural cold stratification; plants form a basal rosette the first year and typically flower and set seed in their second season before declining, so allow self-sowing to maintain a colony.

directions: Plant in rocky, well-drained soil in partial shade on wooded slopes, thinly wooded bluffs, or partially shaded cliff edges, the habitats where this short-lived native wildflower, now also classified as Boechera canadensis, grows wild from the southern Appalachians north to Minnesota and New England. Small, four-petaled white flowers appear on wiry stems in spring, followed by the long, narrow, downward-curving seedpods that give sicklepod its common name. The flowers are visited by small native bees and flies, and the foliage serves as a larval host plant for several native Pierid butterflies, including the falcate orangetip and olympia marble. It behaves as a biennial or short-lived perennial, renewing itself through self-sown seedlings in the lean, rocky soil it prefers, and is best suited to a dry rock garden or woodland-edge planting rather than rich garden loam.

planting.note: Divide established clumps in early spring, or plant container-grown stock in spring or fall, into moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; it spreads by underground runners to form a loose colony within a few seasons.

directions: Plant in cool, moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, recreating the spruce-fir and northern hardwood forests, mountain seepages, and shaded ridges and bluffs where whorled wood aster grows naturally across northeastern North America and south through the Appalachians. Unlike many garden asters, it thrives in genuine forest shade, producing loose sprays of white, pink- or yellow-centered flower heads from late July into October, making it one of the latest native nectar sources available to woodland bees, flies, and butterflies just as most other forest wildflowers have finished for the year. The coarsely toothed, tapering leaves are arranged in a distinctive whorl-like pattern below the flower clusters, giving the plant its common name. It spreads gradually by rhizomes to form an attractive, low-maintenance colony beneath deciduous trees, pairing well with ferns, foamflower, and other true shade natives.
sources: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Nick or file the hard seed coat before sowing, then direct sow after frost danger passes into average, well-drained soil at a woodland edge with a fence, shrub, or trellis nearby for the twining stems to climb.

directions: Plant in average to dry, well-drained soil in partial shade to sun at a woodland edge, thicket margin, or fence line where this twining native legume can climb into surrounding shrubs; it is the only member of the common bean genus native to North America, found naturally in dry woods and thickets from the Mid-Atlantic south into the Southeast. Clusters of small, pink to pale purple pea flowers open in mid- to late summer and are visited by bumblebees and other long-tongued bees capable of tripping the keel-shaped blossoms, followed by slender bean pods in fall. As a legume, its roots fix atmospheric nitrogen, quietly improving soil fertility wherever it grows. It dies back to the root in winter and resprouts reliably each spring, making it a low-maintenance, nitrogen-fixing native vine for a naturalized woodland-edge trellis or fence.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in fall, setting them 2-3 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, circumneutral woodland soil in partial to full shade before hard frost.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, circumneutral soil in partial to full shade on a sheltered slope or stream-side bed, the rich cove forest conditions where this Southern Appalachian endemic grows wild from central North Carolina and Tennessee south into South Carolina, Georgia, and Alabama. In mid-spring, a single maroon to greenish-maroon flower nods on a short stalk beneath the whorl of three broad leaves, held low enough that the strongly reflexed petals are easily overlooked without a close look. Like other Trillium species it is visited by small bees and flies, though its scent and nodding posture suggest it may rely more on crawling or low-flying insects than the upright-flowered trilliums. Because wild populations are considered vulnerable to habitat loss and collection, plant only nursery-propagated divisions, and give it several years to settle in before expecting significant spread.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall into lean, rocky, well-drained soil for natural cold stratification over winter; established clumps are woody at the base and slow to expand, so initial establishment may take a full season.

directions: Plant in lean, rocky, sharply drained soil in partial shade, the rock outcrops, canyon walls, and open conifer and mixed hardwood woodlands of California, Oregon, Washington, Idaho, Montana, Nevada, and Utah where western snakeroot grows wild at mid to high elevations. From a woody-based clump of branching stems, flat clusters of fuzzy, white to pale pink flower heads open in late summer, drawing butterflies and other pollinating insects at a time when many western wildflowers have finished blooming for the season. It is well suited to a dry, partially shaded rock garden or crevice planting alongside other western natives, tolerating thin, mineral soils that would challenge richer-soil perennials. Once established, it needs little supplemental water and resents heavy, wet garden soil.

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall into thin, gritty, fast-draining soil for natural cold stratification; this clump-forming goldenrod spreads modestly by seed rather than aggressively by rhizomes, so initial colonies build slowly.

directions: Plant in thin, gritty, fast-draining soil derived from dolomite or sandstone, in partial shade to sun on a rocky slope or crevice garden, recreating the limestone and sandstone bluffs of the Driftless Area of Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa, and Illinois where this regionally rare goldenrod is found. Unlike the aggressively spreading roadside goldenrods, cliff goldenrod forms a tidy, clump-forming rosette that sends up wiry stems topped with bright yellow flower clusters in late summer and fall, offering a critical late-season nectar source for native bees, honeybees, butterflies, and beneficial wasps, and supporting the larvae of several goldenrod-specialist moths. Because wild populations are uncommon and protected in several states, source only nursery-propagated seed or divisions. Its well-behaved, non-spreading habit and tolerance of thin, dry soils make it a good fit for a crevice garden or dry rocky bank rather than a conventional perennial border.

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall into rich, moist, humus-laden forest soil; like many woodland members of the carrot family, germination is slow and erratic, benefiting from a full winter of cold, moist stratification.

directions: Plant in rich, moist, mesic, often calcareous or mafic-derived forest soil in partial to full shade, the mature closed-canopy hardwood conditions this understory native favors; in several states it is considered an indicator of old-growth forest, turning up reliably on north-facing slopes beneath sugar maple, basswood, and red oak. Small clusters of greenish-white flowers open on branching stems in early summer, and closely related woodland Sanicula species are documented to be visited by both long- and short-tongued native bees along with syrphid flies, a pattern this close relative likely shares. The distinctive bristly, hooked fruits that follow catch in the fur of passing animals for dispersal, a clue to the plant's name. It is not a showy border plant, but as a genuine deep-shade forest-floor native with real ecological value, it is a worthwhile addition to a woodland restoration planting alongside ferns and sedges.

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall into dry, rocky or shaly, well-drained soil for natural cold stratification; plants spread slowly by rhizomes and typically reach flowering size in their second year.

directions: Plant in dry, rocky, shaly, well-drained soil in partial shade, the shale barrens, open woodland clearings, and roadbanks of the central Appalachians from Maryland south into Georgia where this regional native naturally grows. Unlike most sunflowers, which demand full sun, smooth sunflower adapts readily to a dry, lightly shaded garden spot, sending up smooth, dark stems clad in thick, almost plastic-textured leaves. Bright yellow, one- to two-inch flowers open from August into September, offering late-season forage for a range of bees, including the specialist sunflower bees documented across the Helianthus genus. It spreads slowly by rhizomes rather than aggressively, making it a reasonably well-behaved choice for a dry, partially shaded woodland edge where few other tall native perennials bloom so late.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring or early fall, keeping several shoots or growing points per division, and plant into moist, rich hardwood-forest soil in partial to full shade; this species spreads by rhizomes rather than seed in cultivation.

directions: Plant in moist, rich hardwood-forest soil derived from mafic rock, in partial to full shade, recreating the mountain cove forests and canopy gaps of the Blue Ridge Mountains of North Carolina, Tennessee, South Carolina, and Georgia, where this rare native is found. It stands apart from nearly every other Coreopsis species, almost all of which demand full sun, by genuinely thriving in forest shade, spreading gradually by rhizomes into a loose colony rather than a dense mat. Bright yellow, typically-shaped tickseed flowers open atop the broad-leaved foliage in late summer, visited by bees with limited flight ranges that forage close to the forest floor. Because it is uncommon in the wild and rarely offered, source only nursery-propagated divisions, and give new plantings a season or two to settle into their shaded site before expecting significant spread.
sources: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
